Sampling and standard rounding give $(\alpha_0-\varepsilon)$-approximations for nonnegative submodular set functions under one matroid or a fixed number of knapsack constraints.
item.dc:creator: Vaneet Aggarwal, Donglei Du

item.title: Faster Deterministic All-Pairs Shortest Paths with Real Edge Weights
item.description: arXiv:2611.17215v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We give a deterministic algorithm for exact all-pairs shortest paths (APSP), that is, all distances, in directed $n$-vertex graphs with arbitrary finite real edge weights and no negative cycles. Its worst-case running time is $O(n^{2.9929729})$ with the recent rectangular matrix multiplication bound $\omega(1,\tfrac12,1)=2$, and $O(n^{2.99306273})$ with earlier rectangular bounds alone; both improve the deterministic bound $O(n^{2.9997})$ and the Las Vegas expected-time bound $O(n^{2.993805})$. The algorithm runs on a real RAM whose only real-number operations are exact addition, subtraction, and comparison, each at unit cost.
item.dc:creator: Isaac Barouch Essayag (Yohananov), Aryeh Lev Zabokritskiy (Yohananov)

item.title: Running-Time Lower Bounds under FPT $\neq$ W[1]
item.description: arXiv:2611.26080v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We revisit running-time lower bounds historically based on the Exponential Time Hypothesis. We survey bounds that can be recovered from earlier work under FPT $\neq$ W[1] and prove seven lower bounds for graph problems and set systems under the same assumption. The new proofs encode clique choices in few bits and control the target parameter in terms of the encoding. This lets us turn a sufficiently fast algorithm for the target problem into a fixed-parameter algorithm for Clique or Multicolored Clique. In several cases, the new bound matches the function of the parameter in the historical exponent, with the additional requirement that the cutoff for any prescribed saving in the exponent be computable.
item.dc:creator: Hendrik Molter

item.title: Tight Bounds for Distance-Unbiased Sorting
item.description: arXiv:2611.26135v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We study elitist randomized local search for sorting permutations. In this model, each iteration considers a possible exchange of two positions. The entries are exchanged if and only if they are in the wrong order. We introduce \emph{distance-unbiased} selection rules, which may choose an arbitrary distribution over exchange distances but sample uniformly among all pairs at each chosen distance. For static rules, we prove that the optimal worst-case high-probability runtime is $\Theta(n(\log n)^2)$. This establishes the asymptotic optimality of the harmonic sorter within this class and partially resolves an open question of Olesker-Taylor. We then allow the distance distribution to change either according to a predetermined schedule or adaptively using the current permutation and the entire history. Matching upper and lower bounds show that both classes have optimal runtime $\Theta(n(\log n)^2/\log\log n)$. Thus, scheduled adjustments of the distance distribution improve the optimal static worst-case runtime by a factor of $\Theta(\log\log n)$, while full-information adaptation provides no further asymptotic improvement.
item.dc:creator: Mats Bierwirth, Carola Doerr, Johannes Lengler

item.title: Improved Bounds for Directed SSSP in Sparse and Intermediate-Density Graphs
item.description: arXiv:2611.26453v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We give a deterministic algorithm for exact single-source shortest paths (SSSP) in directed graphs with $n$ vertices, $m$ edges, and nonnegative real edge weights. When $m=O(n)$, it runs in $O(n\sqrt{\log n}(\log\log n)^{1/4})$ time. For $m=\Theta(n)$, this lowers the exponent of $\log\log n$ in the bound of Duan, Mao, Shu and Yin from $1/2$ to $1/4$. At intermediate densities, writing $d=m/n$, the same algorithm improves on the bound of Duan et al. when $d\geq 3$ and $d\log(2+d)=o(\log\log n)$. For example, when $m=\Theta(n\sqrt{\log\log n})$, it runs in $O(n\sqrt{\log n}(\log\log n)^{5/8})$ time, lowering their exponent from $3/4$ to $5/8$.
item.dc:creator: Valery (Binyamin), Grishin (Yohananov), Aryeh Lev Zabokritskiy (Yohananov)

item.title: One partition function call to rule them all: Efficiently computing the equilibrium landscape of multiple nucleic acid strands
item.description: arXiv:2611.27945v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: In the nearest neighbour model of DNA/RNA binding, the partition function (PF) is a sum of Boltzmann-weighted free energies of the exponentially large set of secondary structures. Dirks et al. [SIAM review, 2007] gave a polynomial time PF algorithm for $O(1)$ strands, generalising McCaskill [Biopolymers, 1990] single-stranded case. Despite the intuition that PF may somehow encode the entire state space, thus far different approaches were required to solve various energy-landscape prediction problems. For example: finding the minimum free energy (MFE), structure(s) for $O(1)$ strands was open since 2007, and we recently solved [ICALP, 2025] via new techniques. We asked if there is a magnifiable PF algorithm [DNA31, 2025], which we answer here in the affirmative. We give an $O(N^3(c-1)!)$ time, $O(N^2)$ space algorithm, for $c=O(1)$ strands of $N$ bases, the same overhead as Dirks et al. (non-magnifiable) algorithm. However, we show that magnification allows for efficient decoding of the entire landscape, concretely: a single call to the magnifiable PF efficiently solves and improves upon a large number of problems, giving: - MFE in $O(N^3(c-1)!)$ time, $O(N^2)$ space; a considerable improvement over our $O(N^4(c-1)!)$ time, $O(N^4)$ space result [ICALP 2025]. - The first polynomial time algorithm for the multi-stranded density of states problem, in time $O(N^3(c-1)!),O(N^2)$ space. - The first polynomial time algorithm outputting the entire list of energy levels occupied by at least one structure (in time $O(N^3(c-1)!),O(N^2)$ space), and the first algorithms for various energy landscape and counting problems. Our approach unifies the field of energy landscape prediction showing that a single, general, algorithmic framework neatly unifies a large collection of problems that practitioners care about, and required distinct techniques with worse time bounds.
item.dc:creator: Ahmed Shalaby, Damien Woods

item.title: Approximating TSP walks in subcubic graphs
item.description: arXiv:2112.06278v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: We prove that every simple 2-connected subcubic graph on $n$ vertices with $n_2$ vertices of degree 2 has a TSP walk of length at most $\frac{5n+n_2}{4}-1$, confirming a conjecture of Dvo\v{r}\'ak, Kr\'al', and Mohar. This bound is best possible; there are infinitely many subcubic and cubic graphs whose minimum TSP walks have lengths $\frac{5n+n_2}{4}-1$ and $\frac{5n}{4} - 2$ respectively. We characterize the extremal subcubic examples meeting this bound. We also give a quadratic-time combinatorial algorithm for finding such a TSP walk. In particular, we obtain a $\frac{5}{4}$-approximation algorithm for the graphic TSP on simple cubic graphs, improving on the previously best known approximation ratio of $\frac{9}{7}$.
item.arxiv:journal_reference: Journal of Combinatorial Theory, Series B 158 (2023), 70-104
item.dc:creator: Michael C. Wigal, Youngho Yoo, Xingxing Yu

item.title: A characteristic-graph reduction for deterministic L-system inference with classical and quantum-heuristic solvers
item.description: arXiv:2411.19906v4 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: L-systems are widely used to model and simulate biological growth processes, including plant development. Motivated by the broader goal of automating L-system construction, this paper studies the formal deterministic context-free L-system (D0L-system) inference problem in which the input is a finite, noise-free sequence of strings. We introduce the characteristic graph of a string sequence and prove that the existence of a compatible D0L-system is equivalent to the existence of an independent set of a prescribed size in this graph. This gives polynomial reductions from D0L inference to maximum independent set (MIS) and SAT, and hence an exact classical decision route when combined with an exact MIS or SAT solver. We also describe a Quantum Approximate Optimization Algorithm (QAOA)-based quantum heuristic for generating candidate independent sets. This heuristic is not a decision procedure for D0L inference, and failure of the heuristic is inconclusive rather than a certificate of nonexistence. We include computational validation on $22$ generated D0L traces and $8$ negative controls, explicitly incorporate known fixed-identity symbols, and report small statevector QAOA simulations. The quantum component is presented as a proof-of-concept candidate generator, not as a claimed quantum speedup; the immediately useful contribution is the characteristic-graph reduction and the exact classical/SAT decision framework it enables.
item.dc:creator: Ali Lotfi, Ian McQuillan, Steven Rayan

item.title: Learn to Vaccinate: Combining Structure Learning and Effective Vaccination for Epidemic and Outbreak Control
item.description: arXiv:2506.15397v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: The Susceptible-Infected-Susceptible (SIS) model is a widely used model for the spread of information and infectious diseases, particularly non-immunizing ones, on a graph. Given a highly contagious disease, a natural question is how to best vaccinate individuals to minimize the disease's extinction time. While previous works showed that the problem of optimal vaccination is closely linked to the NP-hard Spectral Radius Minimization (SRM) problem, they assumed that the graph is known, which is often not the case in practice. In this work, we consider the problem of minimizing the extinction time of an outbreak modeled by an SIS model where the graph on which the disease spreads is unknown and only the infection states of the vertices are observed. To this end, we split the problem into two: learning the graph and determining effective vaccination strategies. We propose a novel inclusion-exclusion-based learning algorithm and, unlike previous approaches, establish its sample complexity for graph recovery. We then detail an optimal SRM algorithm whose running time is polynomial in the number of vertices for bounded treewidth and a fixed vaccination budget. This is complemented by an efficient and effective polynomial-time greedy heuristic for any graph. Finally, we present experiments on synthetic and real-world data that numerically validate our learning and vaccination algorithms.
item.arxiv:journal_reference: Proceedings of the 42nd International Conference on Machine Learning (ICML 2025), PMLR 267
item.dc:creator: Sepehr Elahi, Paula M\"urmann, Patrick Thiran

item.title: Fermion-to-Fermion Low-Density Parity-Check Codes
item.description: arXiv:2508.15323v5 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Simulating fermionic systems on qubit-based quantum computers often demands significant computational resources due to the requirement to map fermions to qubits. Thus, designing a fault-tolerant quantum computer that operates directly with fermions offers an effective solution to this challenge. Here, we introduce a protocol for fault-tolerant fermionic quantum computation utilizing fermion-to-fermion low-density parity-check (LDPC) codes. Our architecture employs a fermionic LDPC memory, which transfers its state to fermionic color code processors, where logical operations are subsequently performed. We use odd-weight logical Majorana operators to encode fermionic information in the LDPC memory and provide an algorithm for identifying these operators. Explicit code examples exhibit logical failure rates substantially below the physical error rate. We further develop two fermionic lattice surgery protocols to enable state transfer between the memory and processors. Finally, we demonstrate effective error suppression in a simulation of fermionic dynamics using the proposed protocol.
item.dc:creator: Chong-Yuan Xu, Ze-Chuan Liu, Yong Xu

item.title: Kantorovich Distance via Spanning Trees: Properties and Algorithms
item.description: arXiv:2601.08396v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: We study optimal transport between probability measures supported on the same finite metric space, where the ground cost is a distance induced by a weighted connected graph. Building on recent work showing that the resulting Kantorovich distance can be expressed as a minimization problem over the set of spanning trees of this underlying graph, we investigate the implications of this reformulation on the construction of an optimal transport plan and a dual potential based on the solution of such an optimization problem. In this setting, we derive an explicit formula for the Kantorovich potential in terms of the imbalanced cumulative mass (a generalization of the cumulative distribution in R) along an optimal spanning tree solving such a minimization problem, under a weak non-degeneracy condition on the pair of measures that guarantees the uniqueness of a dual potential. Our second contribution establishes the existence of an optimal transport plan that can be computed efficiently by a dynamic programming procedure once an optimal spanning tree is known. Finally, we propose a stochastic algorithm based on simulated annealing on the space of spanning trees to compute such an optimal spanning tree. Numerical experiments illustrate the theoretical results and demonstrate the practical relevance of the proposed approach for optimal transport on finite metric spaces.
item.dc:creator: J\'er\'emie Bigot, Luis Fredes

item.title: Sublinear Time Quantum Algorithm for Attention Approximation
item.description: arXiv:2602.00874v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Given the query, key and value matrices $Q, K, V\in \mathbb{R}^{n\times d}$, the attention module is defined as $\mathrm{Att}(Q, K, V)=D^{-1}AV$ where $A=\exp(QK^\top/\sqrt{d})$ with $\exp(\cdot)$ applied entrywise, $D=\mathrm{diag}(A\mathbf{1}_n)$. The attention module is the backbone of modern transformers and large language models, but explicitly forming the softmax matrix $D^{-1}A$ incurs $\Omega(n^2)$ time, motivating numerous approximation schemes that reduce runtime to $\widetilde O(nd)$ via sparsity or low-rank factorization. We propose a quantum data structure that approximates any row of $\mathrm{Att}(Q, K, V)$ using only row queries to $Q, K, V$. Our algorithm preprocesses these matrices in $\widetilde{O}(\epsilon^{-1} n^{0.5} (s_\lambda^{3} + s_\lambda^{2} d + d) + \epsilon^{-2} s_\lambda d)$ time, where $\epsilon$ is the target accuracy and $s_\lambda$ is the $\lambda$-statistical dimension of the exponential kernel defined by $Q$ and $K$. Each row query can be answered in $\widetilde{O}(s_\lambda^2 + s_\lambda d)$ time. If every row sum of $A$ exceeds $\epsilon\|A\|+\lambda\sqrt n$, then with probability $1-1/\mathrm{poly}(n)$ the answers have Frobenius-norm error $O(\beta\|D^{-1}\|(\epsilon\|A\|_F+\lambda\sqrt n)\|V\|_F)$. Here $\beta=(1-(\epsilon\|A\|+\lambda\sqrt n)\|D^{-1}\|)^{-1}\geq 1$ is close to $1$ when every row sum is much larger than $\epsilon\|A\|+\lambda\sqrt n$. To our knowledge, this is the first quantum data structure that approximates rows of the attention matrix in sublinear time with respect to $n$. Our approach relies on a quantum Nystr\"om approximation of the exponential kernel, quantum multivariate mean estimation for computing $D$, and quantum sampling of the rows of $V$ by their squared norms, with a median over independent samples, for the multiplication with $V$.
item.dc:creator: Zhao Song, Jianfei Xue, Jiahao Zhang, Lichen Zhang

item.title: Efficient Adaptive Data Analysis over Dense Data Distributions
item.description: arXiv:2602.07732v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Modern data workflows are inherently adaptive, repeatedly querying the same dataset to refine and validate sequential decisions, but such adaptivity can lead to overfitting and invalid statistical inference. Adaptive Data Analysis (ADA) mechanisms address this challenge; however, there is a fundamental tension between computational efficiency and sample complexity. For $T$ rounds of adaptive analysis, computationally efficient algorithms typically incur suboptimal $O(\sqrt{T})$ sample complexity, whereas for arbitrary distributions, algorithms with $O(\log T)$ sample complexity are computationally intractable under standard cryptographic assumptions. In this work, we shed light on this trade-off by identifying a natural class of data distributions under which both computational efficiency and logarithmic sample complexity in $T$ are achievable. We propose a computationally efficient ADA mechanism that attains $O(\log T)$ sample complexity, optimal in its dependence on $T$, when the data distribution is dense with respect to a known prior. This setting includes, in particular, feature-label data distributions arising in distribution-specific learning. As a consequence, our mechanism also yields a sample-efficient (i.e., $O(\log T)$ samples) statistical query oracle in the distribution-specific setting. Moreover, although our algorithm is not based on differential privacy, it satisfies a relaxed privacy notion known as Predicate Singling Out (PSO) security (Cohen and Nissim 2020) whenever the number of its possible update transcripts is polynomial in the sample size. Our results thus reveal an inherent connection between adaptive data analysis and privacy beyond differential privacy.

item.title: Packed-Ring Queues: Lock-Free and Wait-Free Concurrent Queues on GPU
item.description: arXiv:2606.01693v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Concurrent queues are a foundational building block of parallel programming. On CPUs, decades of research have produced queue designs with well-understood correctness and progress guarantees -- from lock-free rings to wait-free constructions. On GPUs, where queues increasingly sit on the critical path of device-side task graphs and GPU-initiated I/O, no comparable foundation exists: SIMT execution serializes divergent retries across a warp; tens of thousands of threads contend on the same counter words; the double-width atomics that several CPU designs assume are absent; and GPU memory models are weakly ordered, so the classical algorithms do not transfer unchanged. We present the packed-ring queues (PRQs) -- two linearizable, bounded GPU queues that represent each compound atomic state in one native word of at most 64 bits: (1) PRQ-LF, a lock-free ring whose warp-batched fast path issues one atomic per warp on each of the queue's contended words, and (2) PRQ-WF, a wait-free ring in which peer threads cooperatively complete any operation that falls behind. To the best of our knowledge, PRQ-WF is the first GPU concurrent queue whose wait-freedom is proved as a theorem, with no assumption about how the GPU schedules threads. Across four GPUs from two vendors (NVIDIA A100 and GH200, AMD MI210 and MI300A), PRQ-LF outperforms the blocking Broker Queue by 5.0-20.4x at 32K threads, and PRQ-WF sustains throughput under producer/consumer imbalance where a prior design completes fewer than 0.1% of its attempts.

item.title: Silver Rate Is (Almost) Optimal for Gradient Descent: The Strongly Convex Case
item.description: arXiv:2609.26873v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: We study gradient descent with predetermined nonnegative stepsizes on smooth strongly convex functions. Let $p_{\mathrm{sil}}=\log_2(1+\sqrt2)$ and $\kappa$ be the condition number. We prove the iteration lower bound $\Omega\left(\kappa^{\frac{1}{p_{\mathrm{sil}}}-o(1)}\log\frac1\delta\right)$ for both relative squared distance and relative function error, uniformly over $0<\delta<1$ and sufficiently large $\kappa$. This matches the polynomial exponent of $\kappa$ for the Silver stepsize schedule established in [Altschuler and Parrilo, 2025].

item.title: Four Ways to Stream: Exponential Separations from Random Order and Quantum Memory
item.description: arXiv:2610.06727v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: A streaming algorithm can keep classical or quantum memory, and its input arrives in adversarial or random order. Each resource alone is known to beat the basic model exponentially, but it was not known whether random order can help a quantum algorithm. We compare the four models by exponential space separations: every pair is separated on some problem and tied on another, and the two models with one resource each beat each other on different problems, one direction for random inputs, by concurrent work of Bouland, Ding, and Jain. The new phenomenon is that quantum memory and random order together can be exponentially stronger than each alone. We show this on a streaming version of Hidden Matching in which the bits of $x\in\{0,1\}^N$ arrive many times and $m\le\sqrt{N}$ matching requests must be answered on arrival. In random order a quantum algorithm uses $O(\log N\log m)$ space, while classical algorithms need $\Omega(\sqrt{N})$, and quantum algorithms need $\Omega(m)$ when all data comes before the requests. Two properties explain this. Consumability: answering a request destroys the quantum state. Replenishment: the state can be rebuilt from bits that keep arriving, which random order supplies and a data-first order does not. We prove that one quantum message answering $m$ Hidden Matching requests needs $\Omega(m)$ qubits, a conjecture of Gilboa, Jain, and McClean, for $m\le N^{1/2-\delta}$. The rest comes from Noisy Gap Cycle, a problem of Assadi and Sundaresan: tell whether a graph is a union of cycles of length $k$ or $2k$. With long cycles it needs linear space in all four models: we extend their random-order lower bound to quantum algorithms and obtain the first quantum random-order lower bounds for natural graph problems. With short cycles, $\mathrm{polylog}(n)$ classical bits suffice in random order, but adversarial order requires polynomial quantum space.
